explanations.explanation: Divisions is the word. Paul says he wants "…that there may be no divisions among you and that you may be united in mind and conviction." (1 Corinthians 1:10) That's the whole appeal in one line. He's not asking them to agree on everything under the sun, friend, he's asking them to stop splitting into camps.

Money doesn't come up in this appeal, friend. I know bills are a sore spot for plenty of folks, but Paul's talking about something else. He asks that "there may be no divisions among you," and that they be "united in mind and conviction." (1 Corinthians 1:10) The trouble he's worried about is people splitting apart.

Idols aren't in this verse at all. Paul's appeal is about how the believers treat each other. He says he wants "no divisions among you" and wants them "united in mind and conviction." (1 Corinthians 1:10) So the missing word is divisions, and the whole letter is going to keep circling it.

True. Paul says, "some from Chloe's household have informed me that there are quarrels among you." (1 Corinthians 1:11) He names his sources, too, so nobody can say he's just spreading gossip. The news made it all the way to him, and he's got a response ready.

Chloe's household did report something, and it was quarrels. Paul writes, "some from Chloe's household have informed me that there are quarrels among you." (1 Corinthians 1:11) So this one is True. A report like that is hard to ignore, friend.

Christ it is. Paul lists the four lines people are saying: "I follow Paul," "I follow Apollos," "I follow Cephas," or "I follow Christ." (1 Corinthians 1:12) Notice the last one sits right in the middle of the list of quarrels. Paul says this is what he means by the quarrels, and I'm not going to add a reason he doesn't give.

John isn't one of the names in this list. The four lines Paul gives are Paul, Apollos, Cephas and Christ. (1 Corinthians 1:12) The fourth one is the answer you're hunting for, and it's the name above every other name on that list.

Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, but he doesn't make Paul's list. The four lines are "I follow Paul," "I follow Apollos," "I follow Cephas," or "I follow Christ." (1 Corinthians 1:12) So the fourth team is the one you want.

Not quite, friend. Paul asks, "Was Paul crucified for you?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) He's putting his own name next to Christ's to show how silly the comparison is. The answer he's after is no, so this one is False. Only Christ was crucified, and Paul knows it.

False, and Paul is practically waving his own hand to say so. "Was Paul crucified for you?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) Nobody in Corinth could say yes to that one. It sits right beside his other question, "Is Christ divided?" and the two of them make the point together.

explanations.answer: Were they baptized into his name
explanations.explanation: Right. Paul asks, "Were you baptized into the name of Paul?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) He's checking whether anyone has a reason to put his name on their team. Picture it like a cookie box stamped with the wrong name, friend. It would never go out the door.

explanations.answer: Did they ever meet him in person
explanations.explanation: That question isn't in this verse. What Paul asks is, "Were you baptized into the name of Paul?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) It comes right after "Was Paul crucified for you?" So he's asking about whose name they were baptized into, not whether they've shaken his hand.

explanations.answer: Did they build a church for him
explanations.explanation: Paul never asks about building anything here. His question is, "Were you baptized into the name of Paul?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) He's asking whose name they were baptized into. That's the answer.

explanations.answer: He baptized almost none of them
explanations.explanation: Almost none, that's it. Paul says, "I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius." (1 Corinthians 1:14) Then he adds why it matters: "so no one can say that you were baptized into my name." (1 Corinthians 1:15) The man is thanking God for a short list. Most of us brag about the long one.
It's the other direction, friend. Paul says, "I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius." (1 Corinthians 1:14) That's a very short list. He's glad about it, too.

explanations.answer: He baptized all of them himself
explanations.explanation: All of them would be a LONG list, and Paul is glad his is short. He says, "I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius." (1 Corinthians 1:14) Two names, with one more household added in the next verse. Nobody could call that all of them.

Paul isn't sure, actually, and that's the twist. After naming the household of Stephanas, he says, "beyond that I do not remember if I baptized anyone else." (1 Corinthians 1:16) That's a man saying he doesn't remember, not a man saying he's certain. So this one is False. Honestly, I forget where I set my own chef's hat half the time.

False. Paul says, "beyond that I do not remember if I baptized anyone else." (1 Corinthians 1:16) He's not promising a perfect list, he's being straight about what he remembers. It's a funny way to end a list, friend, and it's honest.

Preach the gospel, yes. Paul says, "Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel." (1 Corinthians 1:17) That's the assignment he points to. Baptism isn't the main thing he was sent for, and neither is a fan club.

Jerusalem isn't mentioned in this verse. Paul says, "Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel." (1 Corinthians 1:17) That's the job he names. It's a clear answer, and it's the one on the card.

This one is tricky, because Paul does mention baptizing. But he says, "Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel." (1 Corinthians 1:17) So baptizing is what he says he was not sent for. Preaching the gospel is his assignment.

explanations.answer: So the cross keeps its power
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says Christ sent him to preach the gospel "not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power." (1 Corinthians 1:17) The power is in the cross, friend, and fancy wording can't add to it. Think of a cookie that doesn't need extra decoration to taste right.

Paul doesn't say anything about the Greeks listening here. His reason is that he preaches "not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power." (1 Corinthians 1:17) The cross keeping its power is the point.

explanations.answer: So no one argues with him
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention arguments in this verse. He says he preaches "not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power." (1 Corinthians 1:17) The reason on the table is the cross and its power. Keeping the peace isn't mentioned.

Foolishness. Paul says, "the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." (1 Corinthians 1:18) Same message, two very different ways of hearing it. And the people who hear it as power are the ones being saved.

A threat isn't the word Paul uses. He says, "the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing." (1 Corinthians 1:18) That's how it sounds to them. For those being saved, it's the power of God.

A riddle is a nice guess, friend, but it's not Paul's word. He writes, "the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing." (1 Corinthians 1:18) A riddle you can still puzzle over. Foolishness is a flat no thank you, and that's the answer.

True. Paul asks, "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?" (1 Corinthians 1:20) He asks it right after calling for the wise man, the scribe and the philosopher. When a question like that gets only silence, it tells you plenty.
That's backwards, friend. Paul asks, "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?" (1 Corinthians 1:20) The way he puts it, God did make it foolish. So this one is True.

Through what was preached, yes. Paul writes, "God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe." (1 Corinthians 1:21) The world looked at that message and called it foolish. God was pleased to save people through it anyway.
Priests aren't in this verse. Paul says, "God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe." (1 Corinthians 1:21) The way he names is what was preached.

Kings don't come up in this verse, friend. Paul says, "God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe." (1 Corinthians 1:21) It's the preaching, not a throne, that he points to.

Christ crucified. Paul says, "we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles." (1 Corinthians 1:23) Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, and Paul doesn't hand either one of them the order they placed. He gives them Christ crucified.

Wisdom is what the Greeks are searching for. Paul says, "Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified." (1 Corinthians 1:22-23) The word but is the turn, friend. He preaches something else.

Signs are what the Jews demand, so it's an understandable pick. But Paul says, "Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified." (1 Corinthians 1:22-23) What he preaches comes after that but.

Stumbling block. Paul says Christ crucified is "a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles." (1 Corinthians 1:23) Picture a toe finding the one chair leg in a dark kitchen. That message trips up people who were expecting something else.

An open door sounds friendly, but it's not Paul's phrase. He says Christ crucified is "a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles." (1 Corinthians 1:23) That's a harder landing than a door swinging open.

A bright light is a lovely picture, but Paul doesn't use it here. He says Christ crucified is "a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles." (1 Corinthians 1:23) A stumbling block is something people trip over.
Not quite, friend. Paul says Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God "to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks." (1 Corinthians 1:24) Both are named. So this one is False.

False. Paul says "to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." (1 Corinthians 1:24) Jews and Greeks are both in the called. The message that tripped them up before becomes power and wisdom for those God calls.

Stronger. Paul says, "the weakness of God is stronger than man's strength." (1 Corinthians 1:25) Think about that for a second. Even God's weakness beats the best human muscle there is, so I'm not going to arm wrestle it.

Weaker would flip the whole line upside down, friend. Paul says, "the weakness of God is stronger than man's strength." (1 Corinthians 1:25) He pairs it with the foolishness of God being wiser than man's wisdom. Both lines point the same direction.
Gentler is a kind word, but it's not Paul's. He says, "the weakness of God is stronger than man's strength." (1 Corinthians 1:25) The comparison is about strength, and the answer is stronger.

It's the other way around, friend. Paul says, "Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth." (1 Corinthians 1:26) So most of them were not powerful. This one is False.

False. Paul tells them to consider the time of their calling: "Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth." (1 Corinthians 1:26) Powerful people weren't the bulk of the church. And that sets up what he says next about who God chooses.

To shame them. Paul writes, "God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong." (1 Corinthians 1:27) It's God's choice, and He picks differently than the world does. Nobody sees that coming, least of all me, a stamper out of a bargain bin.
Teach is a gentle word, but Paul's word is stronger. He says, "God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise." (1 Corinthians 1:27) The text says shame, friend.
Honor would be a nice surprise for the wise, but that's not what the verse says. Paul writes, "God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise." (1 Corinthians 1:27) Shame is the word.

explanations.answer: So no one may boast in His presence
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says God chose the foolish, the weak and the lowly "so that no one may boast in His presence." (1 Corinthians 1:29) Nobody gets to stand there with a trophy. I couldn't brag if I tried, friend, since I was a quarter at the bottom of a bin.

explanations.answer: So the strong will learn to serve
explanations.explanation: Serving is a good thing, but Paul doesn't give that as the reason. He says God chose these "so that no one may boast in His presence." (1 Corinthians 1:29) That's the purpose the text states.

explanations.answer: So the world will copy His ways
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say anything about the world copying God. He says God chose them "so that no one may boast in His presence." (1 Corinthians 1:29) That's the reason on the page.

The Lord. Paul ends with, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." (1 Corinthians 1:31) After a whole stretch about people picking teams around Paul, Apollos and Cephas, that line lands hard. Brag all you want, friend, as long as the Lord gets the credit.

Church is a nice guess, but it's not what's written. Paul says, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." (1 Corinthians 1:31) Boasting in the church would be a lot like those teams in Corinth, and Paul points higher.
Law isn't in this verse, friend. Paul says, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." (1 Corinthians 1:31) The Lord is the one to boast in.
